UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
PROTEST BY 
OFFICE OF THE OHIO CONSUMERS’ COUNSEL 
On August 13, 2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM’s”) filed an application in this 
case to implement a new Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”). PJM requests an 
October 12, 2026 effective data with the IRAS beginning in the 2027/2028 capacity auction 
Delivery Year.   
OCC supports PJM’s proposal to interrupt New Large Loads that connect to the grid 
without sufficient supporting capacity before curtailing residential and other existing consumers.   
However, that proposal does not guarantee that it is the New Large Loads that will be curtailed, 
leaving other consumers at risk of bearing the burden of those curtailments.  Additionally, OCC 
does not support PJM’s proposal to compensate those New Large Loads for interruptions that are 
an inherent condition of their receipt of service without providing adequate capacity for their 
obligations. While the IRAS proposal would establish curtailment conditions for new data 
centers and large loads (at least 50 MW) that lack sufficient capacity, it fails to ensure that 
residential consumers will be protected from the costs or operational risks of IRAS.   
PJM’s proposal will impose excessive rates and curtailments of service on existing 
consumers in Ohio—consumers who are not causing the incurrence of these costs and operating

2 
conditions.1 It will unreasonably shift the risks and costs associated with acquiring new capacity 
for large data center loads away from those very customers onto existing consumers in Ohio and 
elsewhere in PJM.  It also will put existing Ohio consumers at risk of reduced reliability by 
subjecting them to potential curtailments of electric service when large data center load 
customers fail to bring sufficient new generating capacity to satisfy their electricity needs.  
PJM’s proposal essentially places existing Ohio consumers at risk of subsidizing both the cost 
and consequences of resource inadequacy for large data center loads.   
As discussed below, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) should reject 
those portions of the filing that fail to protect Ohio consumers and other consumers in PJM from 
the risks and costs associated with large data center load. PJM’s proposal will result in excessive, 
unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory and preferential rates for existing Ohio 
consumers.   
The Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel is the statutory representative of millions of 
Ohio residential utility consumers, per R.C. Chapter 4911.  OCC actively participates in 
numerous state and federal regulatory proceedings, including proceedings before FERC. OCC 
timely intervened in this case on September 3, 2026.2  Ohio residential consumers may be 
adversely affected if FERC accepts PJM’s proposed IRAS filing without modification. The 
proposal would require other consumers to pay for resource inadequacy risks and related costs 
that they did not cause, i.e., risks and costs associated with obtaining adequate generating 
capacity to satisfy the loads of new Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) and large data center customers.   
1 This Protest is submitted pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Rules of Practice 
and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211. 
2 Doc-less Motion to Intervene in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, filed by Office of the 
Ohio Consumers’ Counsel, available on FERC’s e-library website as Accession Document No. 20260903-5029.

3 
I.
BACKGROUND 
PJM proposes to implement the IRAS proposal starting with the June 1, 2027 Reliability 
Pricing Model (“RPM”) Delivery Year.3 The filing proposes to require New Large Loads to be 
automatically enrolled for IRAS if they fail to bring sufficient capacity to satisfy their capacity 
obligations.4 PJM offers no proposal to address existing large loads that affected the capacity 
auctions run prior to the June 1, 2027 cutoff.   
PJM represents in the filing that it “hosts the largest concentration of data center load in the 
world.”5  It states that its load forecast “predicts peak load growth of 32 gigawatts [(“GW”)] from 
2024 to 2030, 30 GW of which is projected to be from data centers.”6 PJM explains that the 
2027/2028 RPM base residual auction (“BRA”) cleared over 6,600 MW short of the region’s 
reliability requirement, and that the 2028/2029 RPM capacity auction cleared over 6,800 MW short 
of that requirement.7 In other words, PJM represents that the addition of new supply has not kept 
pace with rapid large load demand growth, thus giving rise to the significant tightening of the 
capacity market in recent years and subsequent resource adequacy shortfalls.8  To mitigate the 
potential reliability risks associated with resource adequacy shortfalls, PJM proposes the IRAS “as a 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Proposal of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. to Establish 
Interim Resource Adequacy Service and A Large Load Registry to Address  System Reliability at 7 (Aug. 13, 2026) 
(“IRAS will be available starting with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year, i.e., June 1, 2027”) (hereinafter “IRAS 
Application”). 
4 IRAS Application at 22 (“PJM is proposing Interim Resource Adequacy Service, a new supplemental capacity 
product through which New Large Loads provide a load reduction service that is a tool available to PJM to manage 
resource adequacy shortfalls that would otherwise drive shedding of native loads.”) 
5 Id. at 13. 
6 Id.
7 Id. at 14. 
8 Id. at 13.

4 
mechanism to support reliability while allowing New Large Loads to connect even when new 
capacity supply lags behind load growth.”9
PJM proposes to define “New Large Load” as an “end-use customer load that is either (a) 
a Large Load that goes into service after June 1, 2027, or (b) incremental load in-service after June 
1, 2027, that increases the existing end-use customer load at a single electrical site that, prior to 
such incremental load, did not previously meet the definition of Large Load.”10  After June 1, 2027 
and going forward, PJM proposes that to the extent three consecutive Delivery Years fall short of 
procuring capacity needed to serve all loads on the system, New Large Load shall mean end-use 
customer load that is either (a)  Large Load that goes into service after June 1 of the first Delivery 
Year for which the capacity procurement requirements of the Tariff are not met or (b) incremental 
load in-service after June 1 of the first Delivery Year for which the capacity procurement 
requirements of the Tariff are not met.11 PJM, however, does not explain the justification for the 
cut-off or how pre-existing Large Loads in PJM’s forecasts will be treated.
New Large Load customers would be excluded from the RPM capacity auctions to be run 
starting with the 2029/2030 Delivery Year unless and until these customers can acquire the 
generating capacity needed to serve their loads.12  PJM represents that excluding both the loads 
and capacity of these New Large Load entities from the RPM BRAs would protect residential 
consumers from the costs associated with serving such loads.13  Although the New Large Load 
9 Id. at 13-14.   
10 Id. at 1, n.2. 
11 Id. 
12 Id. at 23. 
13 Id. at 23-24.  The central risk is that this protection works only if the large load is genuinely interruptible.  If a 
state lacks an enforceable curtailment mechanism (see infra) or the large load fails to reduce, PJM will have 
excluded its demand from capacity procurement while still allowing it to consume electricity. Exiting consumers 
would then bear the reliability consequences. There should be a tested, legally enforceable interruption arrangement 
and penalties to secure performance.

5 
customers’ loads would be excluded from the auctions, PJM would still allow these entities to 
connect to and receive electricity from the system.14
If there are resource shortages in any given year, PJM dispatchers would call an IRAS 
emergency before calling on certain other load shedding events.15 PJM dispatchers would direct 
the Electric Distributor(s) in whose zone(s) the New Large Loads that have not procured 
sufficient generating capacity are located to shed load in an amount necessary to address the 
resource shortages.16 PJM anticipates implementing IRAS when “(1) it is no longer able to 
maintain reserves in the RTO or a zone; or (2) there are insufficient resources to keep IROLs 
[Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits] within defined operating limits in order to prevent 
instability, uncontrolled separation, or cascading outages that adversely impact the reliability of the 
interconnection.” 17
 PJM proposes to leave the question of who within each zone would have to shed the load 
needed to restore system reliability to the states.18  In other words, the states would have to set up 
the rules for retail curtailments.19 It is possible under this proposal that an Electric Distributor 
could shut off power to all customers in the zone, even existing consumers, during the emergency 
if a state does not have a program to protect residential and other consumers from these PJM-
directed curtailments.20  Ohio currently does not have such a program.
14 Id. at 13-14. 
15 Id. at 75, 79. 
16 Id. at 79. 
17 Id. at 75. 
18 Id. at 82-85. 
19 Id. at 86-87. 
20 Id. at 90-91.

6 
PJM also proposes to “compensate” the New Large Loads for the interruption through a 
new federal charge imposed on the Electric Distributor.21 PJM likened its proposal here to the 
Pre-Emergency Load Response Program in which it compensates entities willing to discontinue 
service at an early stage of the emergency causing the need for curtailment.22 PJM states that the 
IRAS compensation charge is for “a wholesale load reduction service, but the entities to be paid the 
rate and the loads to be charged to support such compensation must be determined at the state 
level.”23 States could work out an arrangement with the New Large Load that would have the 
New Large Load forego compensation, thus saving other consumers in the zone from having to 
pay those costs.24
Although the IRAS proposal applies only to New Large Loads, PJM proposes to maintain 
a Large Load Registry that would incorporate information on all Large Loads in the region, 
including information that identifies the entities, their peak loads, their locations and Electric 
Distributor zones, their in-service dates, peak load shaving capability, if any, ramp rates, back-up 
generation if any, and other related information.25  PJM proposes to define Large Load as “end-
use customer(s) load that has a cumulative peak load of 50 megawatts or greater at a single 
electrical site behind one or more points of interconnection . . . .”26 PJM further proposes that for 
configurations involving multiple affiliated load facilities or multiple points of interconnection with 
affiliated load facilities behind them, “all affiliated load facilities within a one-mile radius will be 
21 Id. at 99. 
22 Id. at 99-100.   
23 Id. at 104. 
24 Id. at 105. 
25 Id. at 28-29, and 37.   
26 Id. at 31.

7 
considered a single electrical site as further described in the PJM Manuals.”27 PJM represents that it 
will provide access to that information on a confidential basis to authorized state commissions, 
Transmission Owners, the Independent Market Monitor for PJM (“IMM”), Electric Distributors, 
FERC and Load Serving Entities.28  PJM argues the purpose of the Registry is to provide 
transparency and “key information” for state and retail entities.29 But under PJM’s proposal, 
independent state consumer advocates are not permitted access to the confidential registry.    
The filing provides additional details regarding how the proposed new IRAS would be 
implemented.  While OCC is not providing a complete summary of all those details in this 
Protest, it has summarized above the foundational elements that raise significant concerns for 
Ohio consumers.
II.
PROTEST 
The PJM grid must be maintained to ensure reliable and adequate generation and 
transmission services.  FERC has an obligation to ensure that this objective is satisfied in a 
manner that ensures just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential rates for 
services.  In fact, FERC’s primary obligation is to provide consumers a “complete, permanent 
and effective bond of protection from excessive rates and charges.”30
PJM seeks in this filing to ensure that New Large Loads that do not bring sufficient 
generating capacity to the system to satisfy their capacity obligations are placed at risk of 
curtailment when capacity is insufficient to satisfy their needs. This objective is laudable. It  is 
intended to protect existing consumers from the resource scarcity that could result from the 
27 Id.
28 Id. at 28. 
29 Id. at 29, 37-38. 
30 Atl. Seaboard Corp. v. FPC, 397 F.2d 753, 756 (4th Cir. 1968), quoting Atl. Refining Co. v. Pub. Serv. Comm’n of 
N.Y., 360 U.S. 378, 388 (1959).

8 
addition of significant new large loads to the system without also adding significant new 
generating resources.  Indeed, OCC agrees that a reasonable and affordable system to implement 
this objective is urgently needed given the capacity shortages forecast to start with the 2027/2028 
Delivery Year and continue into the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.   
OCC supports PJM’s proposal to interrupt New Large Loads that connect without 
sufficient supporting capacity before curtailing residential and other existing consumers. 
However, OCC is concerned that the PJM’s design of that program will not achieve PJM’s 
intent, leaving consumers other than Large Load and New Large Load customers at risk of 
curtailment.  OCC also does not support compensating those New Large Loads for interruptions 
that are an inherent condition of receiving service without adequate capacity.  Nor does OCC 
support the portions of PJM’s proposal that would leave the details of curtailment 
implementation to the states. 
PJM’s proposed IRAS program, as detailed in its filing, does not deliver the protection 
needed for consumers who are not data centers.  PJM’s proposed program will result in 
subsidized rates for existing Large Loads and New Large Loads in the PJM region. And PJM’s 
proposal will result in excessive and unduly discriminatory rates for existing consumers in Ohio 
and elsewhere in PJM.    
 OCC protests PJM’s filing for three primary reasons.  First, PJM provides no reasoned 
explanation for its compensation proposal. Why should existing consumers whose capacity 
obligations are procured in the RPM auctions have to compensate New Large Loads for 
curtailments when those New Large Loads have not procured sufficient capacity to meet their 
capacity obligations? PJM’s zone-wide compensation proposal should be rejected.  At a 
minimum, if compensation is to occur, (it should not occur) it should be directly assigned to the

9 
participating New Large Load customer causing the shortages or waived by that customer as a 
condition of IRAS service, with no curtailments for or recovery from residential consumers.  A 
strong penalty on New Lard Loads for non-compliance with curtailment directives would ensure 
reliability for the grid in a more just and reasonable manner. 
Second, PJM’s proposed new Large Load Registry unreasonably excludes state consumer 
advocate offices from the list of entities entitled to access the information to be retained in that 
registry. The Registry is designed to contain precisely the information needed by state 
commissions, state consumer advocates, Electric Distributors and LSEs to evaluate retail 
curtailment and cost allocation. OCC is an independent, statutorily-created representative of 
residential consumers.  OCC is not part of the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (“PUCO”).  
Access to the Registry by the PUCO does not give OCC access to that information. PJM’s 
proposal would permit other participants in the industry, utilities and LSEs which may have 
commercial interests in serving the load, to obtain this confidential information. At the same 
time, it would bar access to that information by the statutory representative of the consumers 
potentially charged for IRAS compensation and potentially bearing the interruptions in service 
from curtailments.   
 Third, PJM’s proposal attempts to protect existing consumers from the resource 
shortages resulting from New Large Loads coming on the system as of June 1, 2027.  But PJM 
has not supported the cutoff date, nor explained how pre-cutoff Large Load additions will be 
treated.  Yet  PJM’s filing admits that those Large Loads were primarily responsible for the 
shortfall of capacity procurement under two prior BRA Delivery Years ( 2027/2028 and 
2028/2029).

10 
FERC should reject PJM’s proposal to impose a federal compensation charge for 
curtailments associated with the failure of New Large Loads to bring sufficient capacity to 
satisfy their capacity obligations.  Instead it should (a) direct PJM to adopt strong penalties for 
non-compliance with curtailment directives; (b) expand the list of entities entitled to access the 
Large Load Registry to include state consumer advocate offices; (c) direct PJM to develop and 
file a curtailment plan that addresses emergency priorities for pre-cutoff (June 1, 2027) existing 
Large Load additions, including those associated with already run auctions for the 2027/2028 
and 2028/2029 Delivery Years, i.e., the recent Delivery Years where resource adequacy 
obligations were not met; and (d) grant the additional relief proposed in this Protest.      
A.
PJM’s IRAS proposal to compensate IRAS load for curtailments is patently 
unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory or preferential and fails to 
protect existing consumers.  
There is no justification for compensating New Large Loads for curtailment during 
periods of resource shortages when those loads have failed to bring sufficient capacity to the 
system. PJM’s resource adequacy rules encompassed in the PJM Reliability Assurance 
Agreement Among Load Serving Entities are designed to obligate LSEs to bring sufficient 
capacity to the grid to meet the capacity needs of the consumers they serve.  PJM’s IRAS 
proposal would allow New Large Load customers to connect to the system without an obligation 
to bring sufficient capacity to satisfy their needs.  Treating the removal of the risk New Lare 
Load customers have caused as a separately compensable service and assigning the costs to 
existing consumers improperly shifts to other consumers costs attributable to the conditional 
service furnished to the New Large Load.  In that sense, PJM’s proposal is fundamentally

11 
inconsistent with the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, posted on the White House 
website on March 4, 2026.31
That Pledge, now signed by over 300 organizations including many of the large data 
centers and electric utilities in the nation,32 commits in relevant part that Large Loads will  
1. build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their 
new energy demands, paying the full cost of those resources whether by building, or 
buying from, new or otherwise additive power plants; 
2. pay for all new power delivery infrastructure upgrades required to service their data 
centers, including adequate network upgrade costs to ensure that these expenses are 
not passed on to the ordinary household; and
3. pay these rates for the power and related infrastructure that are brought online to 
service their data centers, whether they use the electricity or not.33
This commitment calls for the imposition of the costs and burdens associated with these very 
large load electricity customers on the large load electricity customers themselves.  
  
In contrast, PJM is proposing that consumers throughout its region, including Ohio 
consumers, will be at risk of: 
1. curtailments if these Large Loads fail to bring the generating capacity needed to serve 
their capacity obligations, especially where state laws may be inadequate to protect them 
from such curtailments;
2. paying generating and transmission capacity costs associated with these new loads; and  
3. compensating these New Large Loads for any curtailments if generating capacity 
shortages occur and PJM must curtail load to retain reliability in the region.   
31 White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge, available at https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-
protection-pledge/ 
32 Data Centers Pay their Way; Ratepayers pay theirs, “A public commitment that hyperscalers, AI companies and 
the utilities and data-center developers behind them will build, bring or buy every kilowatt their facilities need – and 
cover every dollar of the infrastructure that delivers it;” available at https://www.whitehouse.gov/ratepayer-
protection-pledge/ 
33 Supra, n.31.

12 
Although the intent of PJM’s IRAS proposal is to target the New Large Loads with the 
curtailment orders, that intent will not necessarily be achieved.  By design, PJM is proposing 
merely to direct the Electric Distribution in whose zone the New Large Load is located to curtail 
energy usage, and leaves the question of which end use customers will have to curtail to the 
states. But as discussed later in section II.D of the Protest, not all states in PJM have laws 
regarding large load-related curtailments.  Nor do they have laws regarding who pays for the 
compensation that will be required under PJM’s FERC-jurisdictional tariff.  Ohio is one such 
state.  Consequently, OCC protests PJM’s proposal to provide compensation to New Large 
Loads in the event they are curtailed under the new program. At a minimum, if compensation is 
to occur (and it should not), compensation and administrative costs of the IRAS should be 
directly assigned to the participating New Large Load or waived, with no recovery from 
residential consumers. 
The only possible explanation PJM offers for its IRAS proposal is its inapposite reference 
to its non-comparable program for compensating Pre-Emergency Load Response participants.34
This program allows PJM to call upon Pre-Emergency Load Response participants to curtail 
their loads in response to PJM’s issuance of a pre-emergency call for load reductions due to 
growing near-term generating capacity scarcity. Under this program PJM charges the participants 
that underperform or pays those who overperform 50% of the capacity Non-Performance Charge 
rate.35 PJM argues that “[f]rom a customer perspective, the non-performance rate appropriately 
reflects that load paid for capacity but did not get the benefit of the Pre-Emergency Load 
34 IRAS Application at 101, 103. 
35 Id. at 103.

13 
Response Program that PJM called upon at a time when the PJM system was in stressed system 
conditions.”36 PJM proposes to use this rate as the compensation charge for IRAS curtailments. 
But there is a big difference between the two programs that makes compensating New 
Large Loads under the IRAS program unreasonable. The Pre-Emergency Load Response 
participants that are compensated for curtailment during pre-emergency conditions are existing 
customers whose loads are within the load growth forecasts of the RPM auction parameters.  In 
other words, PJM is procuring generating capacity on their behalf.  The system is designed to 
serve them.   
In contrast, the New Large Loads subject to IRAS curtailments will receive accelerated 
access to the grid despite insufficient capacity and are curtailed only because the condition 
supporting that access has occurred.37 Unlike Pre-Emergency Load Response participants, IRAS 
loads will not be included in the RPM auction parameters.38 That means that unlike the Pre-
Emergency Load Response participants, PJM has not procured capacity to serve New Large 
Load capacity obligations. The system is not designed to reliably serve their electricity needs.  
Instead, the IRAS program will rely on curtailment options when generating capacity shortages 
exist.   
It makes sense to compensate existing Pre-Emergency Load Response participants for 
curtailment because their loads are covered by RPM auctions.  They are compensated for the 
inconvenience of having to shed load during emergencies. And their participation in the program 
is voluntary.  But where the capacity needed to serve the New Large Loads is not part of the 
RPM capacity procurement auction to begin with, their participation in IRAS is not voluntary,  
36 Id.
37 Id. at 1. 
38 Id. at 23.

14 
and PJM clearly is not procuring sufficient generating capacity to cover their loads, it makes no 
sense to compensate these New Large Loads for curtailment. Under that scenario, New Large 
Load customers should be curtailed first and without compensation, especially without 
compensation from other customers whose capacity obligations are covered by the auctions.   
These New Large Loads are imposing a huge new burden on the system that is 
unprecedented and unlike the minimal load growth forecasts for existing Pre-Emergency Load 
Response customers. The forecast peak load for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year BRA was 165,954 
MW.39 This is 0.8%, above the forecast peak load of 164,579 MW for the prior 2027/2028 
BRA.40 In contrast, as noted above, PJM anticipates an increase in load due to the influx of New 
Large Load customers of 30 Gigawats (“GW”), or 30,000 MW, from 2024 to 2030.41 An 
increase of 30,000 MW over the current forecast peak load of 164,579 MW for the 2028/2029 
Delivery Year represents a total increase of 18% during that period, or an average of 3% 
annually.42 This impact on resource adequacy is significantly larger than the 0.8% increase in 
load forecasted from the 2027/2028 to the 2028/2029 Delivery Year which includes Pre-
Emergency Load Response customers.   
In other words, it simply is not reasonable to develop IRAS rules based on the Pre-
Emergency Load Response program rules. The impact of the New Large Loads on the system 
has been so significant as to provoke PJM to propose this new curtailment program to protect 
39 2028/2029 RPM Base Residual Auction Planning Period Parameters at 1 (May 12, 2026), available at 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2028-2029/2028-2029-bra-report.pdf 
40 Id.
41 IRAS Application at 13.  The IRAS Application calculates this forecast as 30 Gigawats of new large loads.  Given 
that 1,000 MW is equal to 1 GW, the 30 GW forecast is the equivalent of 30,000 MW of new load in PJM over a six 
year period. Two of those years are now behind us.   
42 30,000 MW represents an 18.2% increase over the 164,579 MW of demand forecasted for the 2027/2028 Delivery 
Year.

15 
reliable electric service in the region during generation scarcity emergencies. While it may have 
been reasonable to compensate voluntary Pre-Emergency Load Response participants to curtail 
loads under the design parameters of that program, it simply makes no sense to pay New Large 
Loads for involuntary curtailments when (1) PJM has not had sufficient notice of their 
interconnection in time to procure new generating capacity on their behalf, (2) they have not 
brought their own sufficient generating capacity to the system to serve their needs, and (3) their 
loads are not included in the RPM parameters.   
To illustrate the unreasonableness of PJM’s proposal, consider the following example. 
The Governor of Ohio is holding a meeting to discuss the importance of affordable electricity in 
the state..  The Governor has invited entities that represent transmission owners and consumers 
to this meeting and tells everyone participating to bring their own lunch. A new entity finds out 
about the meeting, and the day before the meeting informs the Governor that it too is a consumer 
and plans to attend the meeting.  Only this new entity brings 25,000 to 50,000 people with it to 
the meeting.  None of these people bring their own lunch. The Ohio Governor has not included 
these entities in its plans for this meeting given the short one-day notice and does not have 
enough food to serve lunch to all these unanticipated meeting participants.  As a result, the 
Governor must tell the late-notice guests that they cannot share the food of those who were 
invited and who brought their own lunches. Under the PJM IRAS model, the Ohio Governor 
would have to compensate the uninvited guests for going without food during lunch, potentially 
at the expense of the other participants.   
This example is not outrageously exaggerated, nor is it unreasonable. PJM’s filing states 
that the peak loads of 50-MW New Large Load customers are roughly equivalent to the electricity

16 
demands of 25,000 and 50,000 residential homes.43  In effect, the load associated with just one 
New Large Load customer will equal the load of a mid-sized city in the PJM region. The New 
Large Loads anticipated to interconnect to the PJM system that are not bringing their own 
generating capacity (food) will impose a huge drain on the system with relatively short notice, 
especially considering PJM’s three-year forward procurement model for capacity 
auctions.  Existing consumers in Ohio and elsewhere in PJM should not be paying these New 
Large Loads for their “curtailment inconvenience” when these new loads caused the shortage 
conditions by not procuring sufficient generating capacity, and by being unable or unwilling to 
secure that needed new capacity. 
PJM also attempts to justify its proposed compensation scheme by arguing that “[u]nder 
conditions of tightening supply and demand, it is a measured and well-considered response to 
permit the new demand causing the shortfall on the system to interconnect, subject to load reduction 
under limited emergency conditions, but receive compensation for that load reduction.” 44  In 
support, PJM cites to an order on rehearing in a generator interconnection complaint case:   
Tenaska Clear Creek Wind, LLC v. Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 183 FERC ¶ 61,043 at P 24 (2023) 
(“Tenaska II”).  
 That case does not support PJM’s premise that interconnections allowed under limited 
emergency conditions may receive compensation for that curtailment.  In Tenaska II, FERC 
dismissed a complaint in which the generator argued that its facility had been unjustly 
curtailed.45 As PJM correctly notes in footnote 264 of the IRAS Application, FERC found that 
curtailment may be appropriate where a generator begins commercial operation before the 
43 IRAS Application at 35.   
44 Id. at 99 (emphasis added). 
45 Tenaska Clear Creek Wind, LLC, 183 FERC ¶ 61,043 at P 24.

17 
network upgrades needed to accommodate its reliable interconnection to the grid are 
completed.46 But unlike PJM’s characterization of this order, the ruling says nothing about a

Although FERC did not address the question of compensation for the generator 
interconnection curtailments in Tenaska II, it did reject Tenaska’s request for refunds of more 
than $9 million in alleged lost revenues during the curtailment events.47 In fact, FERC’s rulings 
in Tenaska I and Tenaska II support a program of curtailment without compensation where the 
commercial operation of the interconnection customer begins before service can be reliably 
provided because of the need for new infrastructure investment in the region.  
FERC found in Tenaska II that “[s]ubjecting the interconnection customer that causes the 
need for upgrades in this manner ensures that the interconnection customer, bears the system-
reliability burdens that flow from its decision to operate prior to completion of the required 
network upgrades.”48 FERC further found that curtailment in Tenaska II was appropriate because 
the curtailment occurred “on the basis that it [the generator], as an interconnecting facility, was 
subject to limited operation.”49 Like the generator in Tensaka I and Tenaska II, curtailment 
without compensation of a load interconnection customer is appropriate where the customer is 
being interconnected and begins taking service before sufficient generating facilities have been 
constructed to provide reliable service.

before there is sufficient generating capacity to reliably serve their needs.  But, like the tariff in

The IRAS proposal is unjust and unreasonable because it does not contain 
sufficient protections against double recovery by New Large Loads of 
incentive compensation for curtailments. 
The IRAS proposal does not appear to contain rules preventing double recovery by New 
Large Loads under potentially overlapping programs.  For example, the IRAS program is a 
capacity market program, designed to allow New Large Loads to interconnect even in the 
absence of sufficient generation capacity to meet their needs so long as they participate in the 
IRAS curtailment program.  However, these loads may also be eligible for discounted

33 
transmission rates if they take interruptible transmission services or may be eligible for demand 
response payments in the capacity and energy markets. In other words, New Large Load 
customers may be eligible for multiple incentive payments associated with the same curtailment 
event.    
At a minimum, FERC should direct PJM to require New Large Loads to disclose all 
payments received under all PJM market programs for the same curtailment event.  FERC 
likewise should direct PJM to implement tariff provisions that would net additional forms of 
payments for the same curtailment event so that New Large Loads are compensated only once 
for the same curtailment event. Absent such a disclosure obligation and a pricing structure that 
prevents double payment for the same event, there would be no mechanism to ensure that 
consumers in Ohio and elsewhere in PJM do not pay excessive rates for electricity services in 
PJM’s markets.

obligations and related costs to the New Large Loads driving the reliability 
concerns on the grid due to their failure to bring generating assets to the 
system to satisfy their capacity obligations.   
Much of the electric utility industry, large data center loads and even the White House 
agree that existing consumers on the system should be held harmless from the costs and risks of 
New Large Load interconnections to the grid. The White House has even titled its webpage 
addressing this matter “Data Centers Pay their Way; Ratepayers pay theirs.”86

RBP program that “[t]he most important criterion for evaluating proposals to address how to 
reliably serve new data center load is the assignment of the costs and risks associated with LSEs

The IRAS proposal suffers from similar flaws.  It directs curtailment orders to Electric

CONCLUSION 
OCC supports PJM’s proposal to interrupt New Large Loads that connect without 
sufficient supporting capacity before curtailing residential and other existing consumers.  OCC

does not, however, support the proposal to saddle the states with the obligation of ensuring New 
Large Loads bear the consequences of their actions, nor does it support compensating those New 
Large Loads for interruptions that are an inherent condition of receiving service without 
adequate capacity. Such customers should bear the consequences of their decision to take 
conditional service. The associated costs should not be shifted to other consumers, including 
residential consumers.

36 
WHEREFORE, OCC respectfully requests that FERC protect Ohio consumers by  
rejecting the curtailment compensation element of PJM’s Interim Resource Adequacy Service 
proposal in this case; direct PJM to expand the list of entities entitled to access the Large Load 
Registry to include state consumer advocate offices; direct PJM to submit a filing to address 
curtailments that could be associated with Large Loads included in the RPM auctions for the 
2026/2027, the 2027/2028 and the 2028/2029 Delivery Years; and grant the additional forms of 
relief requests in this Protest.
